questions.question: Which has higher specificity: `.card.title.active.large` (four classes) or `#header` (one ID)?
options: The four-class selector, because it has more selectors overall
#header always wins — any number of classes can never outweigh a single ID
It depends on which one appears later in the stylesheet
questions.explanation: Specificity comparison is like comparing version numbers column by column (IDs, then classes, then elements) — it stops at the first column where they differ, so no number of classes can outweigh one ID.

questions.question: What can override a CSS rule marked `!important`?
options: Only another rule that is also marked !important (with equal or higher specificity/later source order among !important rules)
Any selector with higher specificity, even without !important
questions.explanation: !important overrides normal specificity rules entirely, including inline styles — the only way to beat it is with another !important declaration.

questions.question: When two CSS rules have exactly equal specificity, what determines which one applies?
options: The one with the shorter selector
Source order — whichever rule appears later in the cascade (stylesheet order) wins
They are both applied simultaneously, merging their declarations
questions.explanation: Specificity is compared first; only when it's a tie does source order (which rule comes later) act as the deciding factor.

questions.question: Given `.card .title { color: navy; }` (specificity 0,2,0) and `#post-123 .title { color: orange; }` (specificity 1,1,0) targeting the same element, which color applies?
options: navy, because it has more classes
orange, because having an ID in the selector outweighs having more classes
Whichever rule is declared later in the file, regardless of specificity
Neither — the browser would throw an error
questions.explanation: (1,1,0) beats (0,2,0) because specificity compares the ID count first — one ID outweighs any number of extra classes in the other selector.
